summary: Describes Asymmetric Extended Route Optimization (AERO), an experimental way for nodes on a shared multi-access link to find a trusted router and be redirected to a closer on-link neighbor. It avoids the long triangular path through the router while sidestepping operational problems that ordinary redirection can cause on some link types.

eli5.summary: Imagine passing notes through a teacher even though your friend sits right beside you. AERO lets the teacher say, go ahead and hand it over directly, so notes get there faster.

questions: how does route optimization work on multi-access links
how do ipv6 nodes get redirected to a closer neighbor
how does aero prevent packet loss on redirected paths
when should route optimization occur on multi-access links
subtitle: Safer route shortcuts on shared links using mediated redirection.

tldr.problem: On shared multi-access links, nodes often send packets through an intermediate router even when a closer neighbor can receive them directly, creating inefficient triangular paths. Standard redirection techniques cannot safely verify that both the source and destination nodes are willing participants.
tldr.mechanism: Asymmetric Extended Route Optimization (AERO) uses a three-step process: the intermediate router sends a Predirect forward to the destination, which responds with a Redirect back through the router to the source. This ensures both nodes consent and are reachable before direct forwarding begins.
tldr.outcome: Direct paths replace triangular routing only after authorization is verified, avoiding packet loss from filtering, reachability failures, or destination mobility.

today: RFC 6706 defines AERO as an Experimental Protocol. It is designed for multi-access links like NBMA tunnel interfaces, bridged LANs, and large MANETs where standard redirection proves insufficient. The mechanism has been studied in research but has not been widely deployed in production networks. It remains a technique available for implementers dealing with the specific optimization challenges it addresses.

sections.title: The Problem with Indirect Routing
sections.content:
On shared links like wireless networks or bridged LANs, packets often must pass through a trusted intermediate router before reaching a destination. If an ingress node knows only that a router is the default gateway, it cannot know that another node on the link is closer to the destination. The router forwards the packet anyway, creating a long triangular path: from ingress to router to egress.

Standard redirection fails because the ingress has no way to know if the egress is ready to accept direct packets, and the egress has no way to know if the ingress is authorized to use the claimed source address. Simple redirection breaks on links vulnerable to spoofing and cannot detect if the direct path becomes unavailable.
sections.eli5: Without asking first, the far person might refuse the note if they do not trust the sender. Without warning the sender, the path might break or the far person might have moved away.

sections.title: Design Requirements
sections.content:
AERO was designed to solve ten key requirements. Most importantly: it must verify that both the ingress and egress nodes are willing participants (Req 4-5), preventing both spoofing attacks and packets lost to filtering. It must discover when the direct path fails (Req 6) and support mobility, where the destination moves from one egress router to another (Req 8). The mechanism must also handle link-layer address changes (Req 9) and gracefully support network renumbering (Req 10).

Scaling matters too (Req 3): large links with many routers must be able to coordinate through core routers without creating routing loops (Req 7).
sections.eli5: AERO must prove both people agree, find out if the shortcut breaks, remember if someone moves to a new desk, and work when a thousand people are in the room.

sections.title: The Three-Step Handshake
sections.content:
When the intermediate router forwards a packet from ingress node B toward egress node D, it sends an AERO Predirect message forward to D instead of sending a redirect back to B. The Predirect tells D about the ingress node and includes route information encoding which prefixes the ingress can use.

When D receives the Predirect, it validates the message and sends an AERO Redirect back through the intermediate router to B. In this redirect, D commits to accepting packets from B's prefixes, starting a timer (ACCEPT_TIME) for that prefix pair.

The intermediate router forwards the Redirect to B. When B receives it, B creates a forward timer (FORWARD_TIME) and begins sending packets with matching source and destination prefixes directly to D. This asymmetric approach means the forward and reverse paths may use different routers.
sections.eli5: The teacher tells the far student, the near student wants to send notes with this kind of writing. The far student says yes, I will look for notes like that. The teacher tells the near student, yes, send directly. Now they can pass notes between desks.

sections.title: Message Structure
sections.content:
AERO messages are encapsulated in UDP on a dedicated port (8060) so they are distinguished from ordinary ICMPv6 redirects. Each message reuses the ICMPv6 redirect format with a single bit (P=1 for Predirect, P=0 for Redirect) to distinguish message types. All messages include a Target Address (the destination node), a Destination Address (the source node for a Predirect, the destination for a Redirect), and options carrying prefix information and the original packet that triggered the optimization.

Messages are sent with a low IP TTL (8 bytes recommended) to limit their scope and provide quick escape from temporal routing loops. The UDP checksum protects the entire message.
sections.eli5: Messages are notes in a special envelope labeled P=1 or P=0, saying who they came from, who they go to, and what kinds of writing to expect. They have a short lifespan so they do not wander far.

sections.title: Prefix Pairs and Timing
sections.content:
Both ingress and egress nodes maintain prefix pair lists in their neighbor caches. Each pair records a source prefix (from the ingress) and a destination prefix (from the egress) that are permitted together. On the egress, an ACCEPT list records pairs it will accept from the ingress. On the ingress, a FORWARD list records pairs it may send to the egress.

The ACCEPT_TIME timer (recommended 40 seconds) on the egress allows time for the three-step redirection process to converge. The FORWARD_TIME timer (recommended 30 seconds) on the ingress limits how long the ingress sends direct packets. If traffic continues, the ingress sends keepalive Predirect messages every 5 seconds to refresh both timers. If a keepalive receives no reply after three retries, the ingress declares the neighbor unreachable or allows the timer to expire.
sections.eli5: Both remember what kinds of notes are allowed, with timers ticking down. Every few seconds while notes are flowing, the near student checks: are you still there? If no answer comes three times, assume the far student is gone.

sections.title: Handling Movement and Change
sections.content:
When a destination moves from one egress node to another, the egress that loses the destination sends a NULL AERO Redirect message (with target and destination addresses set to null) to the ingress. The ingress deletes the corresponding prefix pair and reverts to sending through the intermediate router. Subsequently, it may receive new AERO Redirect messages from a different egress node, enabling direct paths to the new location.

When an ingress or egress changes its link-layer address, the ingress deletes old FORWARD entries and waits for new redirects with the new address. The egress deletes old ACCEPT entries and sends new AERO Redirect messages using the new link-layer address when it receives new AERO Predirect messages from the intermediate router.

When network prefixes change, nodes mark old prefix pairs as stale and either delete them or allow their timers to expire naturally.
sections.eli5: If the far student moves to a new desk, they send a cancel notice. The near student stops sending directly and waits for new directions. If someone gets a new phone number or email, they each start fresh with new messages.

messages.label: Data packet
messages.note: B sends packet to intermediate router A with source and destination prefixes.

messages.label: Predirect (P=1)
messages.note: A forwards packet to D and sends Predirect telling D about B and the prefix pair.

messages.label: Redirect (P=0)
messages.note: D validates and sends Redirect back, authorizing acceptance of B's traffic.

messages.label: Redirect (P=0)
messages.note: A forwards Redirect to B, authorizing direct packets to D.

messages.label: Direct packets
messages.note: B sends subsequent matching packets directly to D without going through A.
